The thing I was least prepared for was not the language. It was how much of the work is talking. In my first semester I was asked to defend a position in front of fourteen people, in week two, and nobody had warned me. Back home I had always been evaluated on what I wrote. Here I am evaluated on what I say, and on how quickly I can say it. My advice to anybody coming over is boring but I will give it anyway. Do not spend the last six months polishing your grammar. Spend them arguing out loud with somebody who disagrees with you, in English, about something you actually care about. That is the skill. The grammar arrives on its own if you use it enough.

We ran the oldest experiment in the book, the one children play at parties, but with adults and with a written text. Twelve people, each one reading the previous version once and then writing it from memory. What survives is not what you would guess. Numbers go first, almost immediately. Names go second. What survives to the twelfth person is the shape of the story and, above all, anything that sounds like a moral. In four of our five chains the twelfth version contained a sentence that appeared in none of the first eleven, and in every case it was the sentence that explained the point. People do not just lose information. They add the ending it should have had. That is not dishonesty. That is what memory is for.
